title: Atmospheric Pressure and Temperature by City
text:
Readily available weather data can tell us a lot about the long term and short term weather conditions of a location based off of different attributes of the landscape. In this study we are going to be analyzing the relationship between atmospheric pressure and average temperature. Taking 3 different cities into account with varying elevations, climates and locations, we will attempt to understand how average temperature changes with air pressure. Our 3 locations in particular are Mexico City (CDMX), Rexburg, Idaho and Burbank, California. Mexico City has an elevation of 7349 feet. Rexburg has an elevation of 4862 feet. Burbank has an elevation of 600 feet.


Show the code
library(GSODR) #run: install.packages("GSODR") 
# to get the GSODR package. You'll need this package to pull in your weather data.
load(system.file("extdata", "isd_history.rda", package = "GSODR"))
library(dplyr)
library(pander)
library(stringr)
#Run this in your console to see the Country Names you can pick from:
#Search "United States" in the search bar of the top-right corner of the data Viewer that pops up.
#Or search for any other country you are interested in.
#Goal, select the STNID (station ID) for two different weather stations. 
#For example, Rexburg is STNID == "726818-94194"
#Once you have two STNID values selected, go to the next R-chunk.
rexburg <- get_GSOD(years = 2023, station = "726818-94194")
#Run: View(rexburg)
#To see what columns mean, go here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GSODR/vignettes/GSODR.html#appendices

burbank <- get_GSOD(years = 2023, station = "722880-23152")

CDMX <- get_GSOD(years = 2023, station = "766793-99999")

#Then run a similar code to get your station information for your weather stations.
#(If you want to use rexburg, then just use one of the following codes)
#cityName1 <- get_GSOD(years = 2023, station = "yourchoice1")
#cityName2 <- get_GSOD(years = 2023, station = "yourchoice2")

#Finally, join your two datasets together into one dataset:
raw <- rbind(rexburg, burbank, CDMX)
weather <- raw %>%
  mutate(
    name_clean = case_when(
      str_detect(NAME, regex("REXBURG", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Rexburg",
      str_detect(NAME, regex("BURBANK", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Burbank",
      str_detect(NAME, regex("BENITO", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "CDMX",
      TRUE ~ NAME   # fallback: keep original if none match
    )
  ) %>%
  # reorder so the new clean column comes first
  select(name_clean, everything(), -NAME)


In performing this analysis we must create an equation to map our data onto. This shape takes the form of a line that can be represented in the following equation.

  Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 C_{i2} + \beta_3 C_{i3} + \beta_4(P_i * C_{i2}) + \beta_5(P_i * C_{i3}) + \epsilon_i
 Y_i represents the y value of the equation and the average temperature of the city.
Beta_0, Beta_2 and Beta_4 represent the various y intercepts for each city. Meaning that if the atmospheric pressure were 0, where might the average temperature lie. This idea helps us to test if our findings are true using the following hypothesis

  H_o: \beta_0 = \beta_2 = \beta_4\\
  H_a: \text {At least one } \beta_j \text { different}

Beta_1, Beta_3 and Beta_5 represent the slopes of each of the lines. If each city had a different rate of change to the relationship between average temperature and atmospheric pressure we would see it occur in these variables. This knowledge will help us with another hypothesis shown below.

  H_o: \beta_1 = \beta_3 = \beta_5\\
  H_a: \text {At least one } \beta_j \text { different}

We will also use an alpha of 0.05 so determine if a certain statistic is significant or not. 
  \alpha = 0.05

Conclusion

Our results showed us the significant relationship they had at a city with lower altitude but could not find a relationship between the two at higher altitudes. We can safety say that in Burbank, CA, atmospheric pressure and average temperature have a negative linear relationship. For further study it might be pertinent to filter out all data but from Burbank, CA so that we might know with a higher certainty the relationship between the two without the data from the other cities to influence the diagnostic plots as we have seen in this analysis.

title: Which Paper Airplane Flies Farthest?
text: The Boeing Engineering team has tasked us with finding out which paper airplane design is “best”. Such an experiment is important so that they may be able to find better ways in which we can design airplanes in the future. Now the “best” paper airplane design is a very subjective idea. It could be measured by flight time or flight distance. The experiment could also be affected by a myriad of factor including wind speed and angle of initial attack. In order to complete a proper experiment and reveal actual, verifiable and accurate results I took on this problem by designing 3 different paper airplanes. The design would be the experimental variable which we act upon. I measured the “best” paper airplane in terms of flight distance because I wanted to see if the designs themselves did anything to increase flight efficiency. This will be our response variable.

title: Water Polo Shot Success by Distance
text: In this analysis, the goal is to understand how the distance from the goal affects the likelihood that a water polo shot is successful or stated as a question, “Does distance affect whether a water polo player will make a shot in goal or not?” Each point represents a real shot attempt, recorded with a binary outcome. That the player scored (1) or did not score (0). Since the response variable is binary, a logistic regression model is appropriate. This approach allows us to estimate how the probability of scoring changes as the shooting distance increases. This model can show whether closer shots truly have a higher probability of success, and how sharply that probability declines as players shoot from farther away. Ultimately, the logistic model provides a way to quantify a common coaching belief in water polo: the farther the shot, the lower the chance it goes in.

title: Water Polo Shot Success by Distance
text:
Hypothesis
In our analysis, the probability that a shot is made based on the distance the player is from the goal is shown by this equation. 
  P(Y_i = 1|x_i) = \frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i}}{1+e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i}} = \pi_i

Using this model we can test if distance to the goal actually affects whether a shot is made or not. B_1 representing the effect that distance has on shooting percentage. We will be using an alpha of 0.05 to measure significance. Our null hypothesis stating that distance from the goal holds no effect on the probability of a successful shot. While our alternative hypothesis states that there is a relationship between the two. 
  H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \\
  H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\\
  \alpha = 0.05

title: Water Polo Shot Success by Distance
text:
Conclusion
Based on the logistic regression results, there is statistical evidence that distance from the goal has a meaningful effect on a player’s chance of scoring. The negative slope in the model indicates that as a shooter moves farther away from the goal, the probability of scoring steadily decreases. The p-value for the distance coefficient was well below the 0.05 significance level, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that distance truly influences shot success. While the model does not perfectly predict outcomes, as shown by the low goodness-of-fit value, it still captures an important overall trend: close-range shots are much more likely to result in goals than long-range shots. In practical terms, this supports common coaching strategy in water polo, emphasizing high-percentage opportunities taken near the goal rather than low-percentage attempts from the perimeter. The analysis shows that distance matters, and the farther the shot, the slimmer the odds of scoring.

title: Gun Deaths by Age, Intent, and Season
text:
A client planning public-service commercials wanted to know who to reach, what message to use, and when to air them. Using FiveThirtyEight’s data on U.S. gun deaths, I broke deaths down by age, race, intent (homicide vs. suicide), and season, and wrote each chart’s takeaway for that audience.


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)




Show the code
df <- read_csv("https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/guns-data/raw/master/full_data.csv")


In the interactive data I discovered the animations and the different styles of displaying the data. It was also interesting to see how they filtered and categorized the data using different arcs and colors.


Show the code
nona <- df %>% 
  filter(!is.na(intent) & !is.na(sex) & !is.na(age) & !is.na(race) & !is.na(month)) 




Show the code
nona <- nona %>%
  mutate(Age = ifelse(age < 15, "Under 15",
          ifelse(age >= 15 & age <= 34, "15 - 34",
          ifelse(age >= 35 & age <= 64, "35 - 64", "65+"))))

nona$Age <- factor(nona$Age, levels = c("Under 15", "15 - 34", "35 - 64", "65+"))




Show the code
ggplot(nona, mapping = aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_bar()









Here in this visualization we can see the different age demographics that are dying from gun-related incidents. The largest group is young adults from ages 15–34. This shows that younger adults are an important group for the client to focus on. Commercials aimed at younger people could focus on gun safety, violence prevention, and making safer choices.


Show the code
ggplot(nona, mapping = aes(x = race)) + 
  geom_bar()









This graph shows the total number of gun deaths by race. This helps the client see which racial groups have the highest number of deaths in the dataset. The client should be careful not to blame any group, but this information can help them make commercials that are more specific to communities that are affected. The message should focus on prevention, safety, and support.


Show the code
cleanintent <- nona %>% filter(intent != "Unknown")




Show the code
ggplot(cleanintent, mapping = aes(x = Age, fill = intent)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")









We can clearly see that different age groups are affected by different types of gun deaths. Younger adults have more homicide deaths, while older adults have more suicide deaths. This is important because the client should not use the same message for every age group. Commercials for younger adults could focus more on violence prevention, while commercials for older adults could focus more on suicide prevention and safe gun storage.


Show the code
season <- nona %>%
  mutate(Season = case_when(month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
      month %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Spring",
      month %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "Summer",
      month %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall"))

season_deaths <- season %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  summarize(total_deaths = n(), .groups = "drop")




Show the code
ggplot(season_deaths, aes(x = Season, y = total_deaths)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Total Gun Deaths by Season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Total Deaths")









This graph shows which season has the most gun deaths. This helps the client know when commercials might be most needed. If one season has more deaths, the client could run more commercials during that time. This gives the client a simple way to think about when prevention messages should be strongest.


Show the code
season_intent <- season %>% 
  filter(intent != "Unknown") %>% 
  group_by(Season, intent) %>% 
  summarize(total_deaths = n())




Show the code
ggplot(season_intent, aes(x = Season, y = total_deaths, fill = intent)) + 
  geom_col(position = "dodge")









This graph shows what kind of gun deaths happen in each season. This helps the client know what the commercials should talk about. For example, some commercials could focus on suicide prevention, while others could focus on violence prevention. The client can use this graph to match the commercial message to the biggest problem in each season.


Show the code
season_age <- season %>% group_by(Season, Age) %>% 
  summarize(total_deaths = n())




Show the code
ggplot(season_age, aes(x = Season, y = total_deaths, fill = Age)) + 
  geom_col(position = "dodge")









This graph shows which age groups have the most gun deaths in each season. This helps the client know who the commercials should be made for. If younger adults have more deaths, the client could make commercials aimed at younger people. If older adults are also high, then the client could make a different commercial about suicide prevention and safe gun storage.

title: The Housing Crisis Through Building Permits
text:
How hard did the 2008 housing crisis hit new construction? Using U.S. Census building permit data, I calculated the percent change in single-family permits from 2006 to 2010. I mapped it by state with sf and then zoomed into California counties, using a diverging color scale so that declines and increases stand out.


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(USAboundaries)
library(geofacet)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
library(buildings)

data("permits")




Show the code
state_permits <- permits %>%
  filter(variable == "Single Family")




Show the code
california_county_permits <- permits %>%
  filter(variable == "Single Family") %>%
  filter(StateAbbr == "CA")




Show the code
us_states <- us_states() %>%
  filter(stusps != "PR" & stusps != "HI" & stusps != "AK")
ca_counties <- us_counties(states = "California")




Show the code
state_permits <- state_permits %>%
  mutate(state_fips = str_pad(state, width = 2, pad = "0"))

california_county_permits <- california_county_permits %>%
  mutate(state_fips = str_pad(state, width = 2, pad = "0")) %>% 
  mutate(county_fips = str_pad(county, width = 3, pad = "0")) %>% 
  mutate(full_county_fips = paste0(state_fips, county_fips))




Show the code
state_permits_map <- us_states %>%
  mutate(state_fips = statefp) %>%
  left_join(state_permits, by = "state_fips")

ca_county_permits_map <- ca_counties %>%
  mutate(full_county_fips = geoid) %>%
  left_join(california_county_permits, by = "full_county_fips")




Show the code
state_change <- state_permits %>%
  group_by(state_fips, StateAbbr, year) %>% 
  summarize(total_permits = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2006, 2010)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = total_permits, 
    names_prefix = "permits_") %>%
  mutate(percent_change = (permits_2010 - permits_2006) / permits_2006)




Show the code
state_change_map <- us_states %>%
  mutate(state_fips = statefp) %>%
  left_join(state_change, by = "state_fips")




Show the code
ggplot(state_change_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = percent_change), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "red", mid = "white", high = "blue", midpoint = 0,
    labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Single Family Building Permits Nationwide",
    subtitle = "% change from '06 to '10",
    fill = "% change") +  
  theme_classic()











Show the code
ca_county_change <- california_county_permits %>%
  group_by(full_county_fips, year) %>% 
  summarize(total_permits = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2006, 2010)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = total_permits, 
    names_prefix = "permits_") %>%
  mutate(percent_change = (permits_2010 - permits_2006) / permits_2006)




Show the code
ca_county_change_map <- ca_counties %>%
  mutate(full_county_fips = geoid) %>%
  left_join(ca_county_change, by = "full_county_fips")




Show the code
ggplot(ca_county_change_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = percent_change), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "red", mid = "white", high = "blue", midpoint = 0, 
    labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Single Family Building Permits by County in CA",
    subtitle = "% change from '06 to '10",
    fill = "% change") +
  theme_classic()









These graphics show the trend of single family building permits in the US and California specifically from 2006-2010 following and after the mortgage crisis. In each graph we can observe that the largest majority of geographical areas at both the state and national level fell by a large margin, with only very specific and select places not falling too much or increasing in one particular area.
In organizing this data I chose to focus on California because it is my home state and because it has San Jose, California which is a huge place for Silicon Valley which seemed to do alright despite the crisis. In filtering the data I only included the continental united states. I also wanted to emphasize the the negative and positive trends over everything else so that’s why no change is a neutral white.

title: Traffic Sign Recognition with a CNN
text:
Approach

Augmentation: random rotation (±15°), shifts, shear, zoom, and a custom HSV brightness adjustment. These simulate signs seen at different angles and in different lighting.
Architecture: three convolutional layers (32 → 64 → 64 filters) with max pooling, then a dense layer with a 43-way softmax output.
Pipeline: Keras ImageDataGenerator streams images from disk with an 80/20 train/validation split, and the trained model predicts the holdout set for competition scoring.

model = models.Sequential([
    layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', input_shape=(100, 100, 3)),
    layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),
    layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu'),
    layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),
    layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu'),
    layers.Flatten(),
    layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    layers.Dense(43, activation='softmax'),
])

title: Traffic Sign Recognition with a CNN
text:
Lessons learned
When I stopped training early, the saved model collapsed to predicting a single class on the holdout set. The cause was a loss-function mismatch: from_logits=True combined with a softmax output layer. The fix is to compile with from_logits=False and add an EarlyStopping callback that restores the best weights. Tracking that down taught me to check a model’s prediction distribution, not just its accuracy, before submitting.

title: Forecasting Bike-Share Demand with a Neural Network
text:
Approach

Feature prep: one-hot encoded season and weather situation, dropped the date and target columns, and scaled every feature with MinMaxScaler, fit only on the training split.
Architecture: Dense(128) → Dropout → Dense(256) → Dense(64, leaky ReLU) → Dense(1, ReLU), so predictions can’t go below zero.
Tuning: wrapped the model with scikeras.KerasRegressor and searched over activation, dropout rate, and batch size with 3-fold cross-validation.

def create_model(optimizer='adam', dropout_rate=0.5, activation='relu'):
    model = Sequential()
    model.add(Input(shape=(len(X_train[0]),)))
    model.add(Dense(128, activation=activation))
    model.add(Dropout(dropout_rate))
    model.add(Dense(256, activation=activation))
    model.add(Dense(64, activation='leaky_relu'))
    model.add(Dense(1, activation='relu'))
    model.compile(loss='mse', optimizer=optimizer)
    return model

param_grid = {
    'model__dropout_rate': [0.3, 0.5, 0.7],
    'model__activation': ['relu', 'tanh'],
    'batch_size': [16, 32, 64],
    'epochs': [3],
}
grid = GridSearchCV(KerasRegressor(model=create_model), param_grid,
                    scoring='neg_mean_squared_error', cv=3)

title: Automated ETL Pipelines with Apache Airflow
text:
Engineering decisions

Idempotent loads. MERGE statements keyed on date and entity mean a rerun or backfill updates rows instead of duplicating them.
Secrets stay out of code. Every credential, including the Snowflake key-pair, the SSH and SFTP passwords, and the Finnhub API key, is read from environment variables. The repository only includes an example.env template.
Shared helpers. dags/utils.py centralizes Snowflake connections (password or private-key auth), the MongoDB SSH tunnel, and API-key lookup, so each DAG stays short.
Testable outside Airflow. Each DAG falls back to plain Python decorators when Airflow isn’t installed, so the extract and transform logic can be run and debugged locally.
Visible history. The archive/ folder keeps earlier versions (v1 → v3) to show how the pipelines evolved, from a single script to modular tasks with retries and backfill.

An excerpt from the weather DAG, showing the schedule and the upsert from a temporary staging table:

    schedule="0 19 * * 0",          # every Sunday, 12:00 PM Mountain Time

    catchup=True,                   # backfill any missed weeks
    tags=["weather", "etl", "snowflake", "openmeteo"],
)

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)


Which origin airport is best to minimize my chances of a late arrival when I am using Delta Airlines?

delta_flights <- flights %>%
  filter(carrier == "DL") %>%
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) %>%
  mutate(late_15 = arr_delay > 15)




Show the code

  group_by(origin) %>%
  summarize(total_flights = n(),
    avg_arrival_delay = mean(arr_delay),

Advanced Salary Distribution by Position (with Case Statement):
* Write an SQL query that provides a summary table showing the average salary for players in each position (e.g., pitcher, catcher, outfielder) across all years. Include the following columns:

    * position
    * average_salary
    * total_players
    * highest_salary  

* The highest_salary column should display the highest salary ever earned by a player in that position. If no player in that position has a recorded salary, display “N/A” for the highest salary.  

* Additionally, create a new column called salary_category using a case statement:  

    * If the average salary is above $1 million, categorize it as “High Salary.”  
    * If the average salary is between $500,000 and $1 million, categorize it as “Medium Salary.”  
    * Otherwise, categorize it as “Low Salary.”  

* Order the table by average salary in descending order.
* Print the top 10 rows of this summary table.  
Using the subquery and the case function we are able to make a new table to call upon in our query which allows us to do further calculations that are not in the data. It seems that first baseman make the most money of anyone on the team.


Show the code
# Include and execute your code here
q = """
    SELECT t.POS AS position,
        ROUND(AVG(s.salary), 2) AS average_salary,
        COUNT(DISTINCT s.playerID) AS total_players,
        MAX(s.salary) AS highest_salary,

title: Combining Five Height Datasets
text:
Is everyone getting taller? To find out, I combined five height studies published in five different formats: two Stata files, a zipped dBase (DBF) file, a CSV, and an SPSS survey. Each one used different column names, units, and age definitions. I standardized birth year and height (in inches and centimeters), kept only the comparable fields, and stacked the sources into a single tidy dataset.


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(foreign)
library(readr)




Show the code
one <- read_dta('https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/heights/germanconscr.dta')

two <- read_dta('https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/heights/germanprison.dta')

zip_path <- file.path(tempdir(), 'Heights_south-east.zip')
download.file('https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/heights/Heights_south-east.zip', zip_path, mode = 'wb')
unzip(zip_path, exdir = tempdir())
three <- read.dbf(file.path(tempdir(), 'B6090.DBF'))
three <- as_tibble(three)

four <- read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hadley/r4ds/main/data/heights.csv')

five <- read_sav('https://www.ssc.wisc.edu/nsfh/wave3/NSFH3%20Apr%202005%20release/main05022005.sav')




Show the code
cleanone <- one %>%
  select(bdec, height) %>%
  rename(Birth_Year = bdec, Height_cm = height) %>%
  mutate(Source = "German Conscription Data"  )

cleantwo <- two %>%
  select(bdec, height) %>%
  rename(Birth_Year = bdec, Height_cm = height) %>%
  mutate(Source = "German Prison Data")

cleanthree <- three %>%
  select(GEBJ, CMETER) %>%
  rename(Birth_Year = GEBJ, Height_cm = CMETER) %>%
  mutate(Source = "Southeast German Data")

cleanfour <- four %>%
  filter(sex == "male") %>%
  transmute(Birth_Year = 1950 - age, Height_cm = height * 2.54, Source = "Labor Statistics Data")

cleanfive <- five %>%
  transmute(Birth_Year = 1900 + as.numeric(DOBY),
    Height_feet = as.numeric(RT216F),
    Height_inches = as.numeric(RT216I),
    Source = "Wisconsin Data") %>%
  filter(Height_feet >= 4,
    Height_feet <= 7,
    Height_inches >= 0,
    Height_inches <= 11) %>%
  mutate(Height_cm = ((Height_feet * 12) + Height_inches) * 2.54) %>%
  select(Birth_Year, Height_cm, Source)




Show the code
all_heights <- bind_rows(cleanone, cleantwo, cleanthree, cleanfour, cleanfive) %>%
  drop_na(Birth_Year, Height_cm, Source)

all_heights

In the cleaning of this data I decided to get rid of everything but things involving birth years and observed heights. So I kept all ages, birthday years and heights in any metric. I had to do some manipulating to get the proper formats for inches and centimeters and for birth years but then combining them was relatively easy. Once they were all cleaned up it didn’t take long to get all of it into one dataset.


Show the code
ggplot(all_heights, aes(x = Birth_Year, y = Height_cm, color = Source)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Male Height by Birth Year",
    color = "Study") +
  theme_bw()









In the old data the trend was that people were getting taller over time. While data from the last activity backed this theory up, it was only one side of the story. We only had data at the time from one time period in one country. This let us see that people in Germany during the years 1810-1980 were in fact on average getting taller, but we can see a different trend in the data that we have availible now.
With this current data we can see many different peoples in different geographic locations and time periods mapped out over time. With this more cumulative dataset we can see that while people in Germany from 1810-1980 were in fact getting taller, the larger population of the world has not followed the same trend if you go back far enough. This is important because while it is interesting to follow trends and understand things within context windows, one cannot make a full generalization on everything based on such myopic data.

title: Star Wars Survey Coding Challenge
text:
The challenge
In a timed coding challenge, I had to clean FiveThirtyEight’s Star Wars fan survey and recreate two charts from their article. The survey ships as three messy files: multi-response questions, single-response questions, and a wide table with long, machine-generated column names. The work was to rename and select the useful fields, filter to respondents who had seen all six films, derive each person’s favorite film from their rankings, and rebuild the published charts.

title: Star Wars Survey Coding Challenge

    exposure = seen_any6,
    fan = fan_yn,
    expanded = fan_expanded,
    startrek = fan_startrek) %>% 
  select(c(1,7,8,9,10,11)) %>% 
  drop_na(shot_first)

title: Picking the Best Day for a Chipotle Promotion
text:
Chipotle wants to run a one-day promotion on its slowest day. In the raw data, each restaurant’s weekday traffic is stored as one text field that lists all seven days and their visit counts. I wrote two small parsing functions with stringr, mapped them over every location with purrr, and unnested the result into a tidy table so visits could be compared across days.


Show the code
library(tidyverse)




Show the code
chipotle <- read_csv("https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/chipotle_reduced.csv")




Show the code
table_maker <- function(extractor) {
  days <- str_extract_all(extractor,
    "Monday|Tuesday|Wednesday|Thursday|Friday|Saturday|Sunday")[[1]]
  
  amount <- str_extract_all(extractor, "\\d+")[[1]] %>%
    as.integer()
  
  tibble(days = days, amount = amount)
}




Show the code
highest_day <- function(extractor) {
  df <- table_maker(extractor)
  
  df %>%
    filter(amount == max(amount)) %>%
    pull(days) %>%
    paste(collapse = ", ")
}




Show the code
weekday_levels <- c("Monday", "Tuesday","Wednesday",
  "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")




Show the code
chipotle_nested <- chipotle %>%
  mutate(day_visits = map(popularity_by_day, table_maker),
    busiest_day = map_chr(popularity_by_day, highest_day))




Show the code
saveRDS(chipotle_nested, file = file.path(tempdir(), "chipotle_nested.rds"))




Show the code
chipotle_visits_long <- chipotle_nested %>%
  select(placekey, city, region, day_visits) %>%
  unnest(day_visits) %>%
  mutate(days = factor(days, levels = weekday_levels))




Show the code
visits_by_weekday <- chipotle_visits_long %>%
  filter(!is.na(days), !is.na(amount)) %>%
  group_by(days) %>%
  summarize(total_visits = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")




Show the code
ggplot(visits_by_weekday, aes(x = days, y = total_visits)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_visits)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Total Chipotle Visits by Day of the Week",
    y = "Total visits") +
  theme_minimal()









In the long version of the dataset, one row represents one weekday at one Chipotle restaurant. Each restaurant can have up to seven rows, with one row for each day of the week. The amount column shows how many visits that restaurant had on that weekday. In the busiest-day summary, one row represents one weekday and the number of restaurants where that day had the highest visit count.
The total visit graph shows that Sunday has the lowest traffic, with 116,884 visits. Monday is also fairly slow, but Sunday is clearly the weakest day. Based on this graph, Chipotle should consider running the promotion on Sunday to help bring in more customers on a slower day.


Show the code
busiest_day_counts <- chipotle_nested %>%
  select(placekey, busiest_day) %>%
  filter(!is.na(busiest_day), busiest_day != "") %>%
  separate_rows(busiest_day, sep = ", ") %>%
  mutate(busiest_day = factor(busiest_day, levels = weekday_levels)) %>%
  count(busiest_day, name = "store_count")




Show the code
ggplot(busiest_day_counts, aes(x = busiest_day, y = store_count)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = store_count), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Busiest Day at Chipotle Restaurants",
    y = "Number of restaurant locations") +
  theme_minimal()









The busiest-day graph also points to Sunday as the best promotion day. Sunday is the busiest day for only 31 restaurants, which is lower than every other weekday. Friday is already the busiest day for 1,053 restaurants, so it would make less sense to use the promotion on a day that is already doing well.

text:
Final Recommendations

Sunday had the fewest total visits and was also the least common busiest day among individual restaurant locations. Another clear pattern is that Friday is the strongest day overall, with the highest total visits and the largest number of restaurants where it is the busiest day. This means Chipotle probably does not need to use the promotion on Friday.

title: Car Wash Sales vs. Temperature
text:
Does temperature drive car wash sales? I converted transaction timestamps from UTC to local time, removed invalid sales, and rolled them up to the hour. Then I pulled hourly weather observations for the Rexburg airport with the riem package and joined them to sales by hour.


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(riem)
library(scales)




Show the code
carwash_raw <- read_csv("https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/carwash.csv")




Show the code
carwash <- carwash_raw %>%
  mutate(UTC = ymd_hms(time, tz = "UTC"),
    local = with_tz(UTC, tzone = "America/Boise"))




Show the code
ggplot(carwash, aes(x = amount)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)









After inspecting the data, I decided to remove rows with missing time values, missing sale amounts, and negative sale amounts. I did not remove high sales just because they were high, because a large transaction could still be a real sale.


Show the code
carwash_clean <- carwash %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(local),
    !is.na(amount),
    amount >= 0
  )




Show the code
carwash_hourly <- carwash_clean %>%
  mutate(sales_hour = ceiling_date(local, unit = "hour"))




Show the code
date_start <- min(as_date(carwash_hourly$sales_hour))
date_end <- max(as_date(carwash_hourly$sales_hour))

rexburg_weather_raw <- riem_measures(station = "RXE", date_start = date_start, date_end = date_end)




Show the code
rexburg_weather_hourly <- rexburg_weather_raw %>%
  mutate(weather_time_local = with_tz(valid, tzone = "America/Boise"), 
         sales_hour = ceiling_date(weather_time_local, unit = "hour"))




Show the code
carwash_weather <- carwash_hourly %>%
  left_join(rexburg_weather_hourly, by = "sales_hour")




Show the code
carwash_weather_clean <- carwash_weather %>%
  filter(!is.na(tmpf))%>%
  mutate(hour_of_day = hour(sales_hour))




Show the code
ggplot(carwash_weather_clean, aes(x = hour_of_day, y = amount, color = tmpf)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Wash Sales by Hour of Day",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Total car wash sales per hour",
    color = "Temperature (F)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









From the data we can see that the car wash has specific operating hours. This helps us to determine now when during those operating hours temperature and sales begin to influence one another. There seems to be no correlation of temperature and sales during operating hours. Sales peak in the morning, the middle of the day and the afternoon on different days. It would stand to reason though, from looking at the density of the data points on hotter days, that the warmer and more comfortable the day is, the more likely people are to go get a car wash.

title: Portlight: Local Network Security Dashboard
text:
Portlight answers a simple question: what on my computer is listening on the network, where is it talking to, and what deserves a closer look? A Windows PowerShell collector reads sockets, processes, services, and firewall profiles. It uploads a snapshot to a locked-down Docker container, which applies transparent review rules and serves a dashboard at 127.0.0.1:9090.



Portlight dashboard (demo mode with synthetic data)


I built it for my AI 101–102 course as a human-in-the-loop project. The tool observes the machine and explains its evidence, but it never changes firewall settings or terminates processes on its own.

text:
Architecture






flowchart TB
    W[Windows socket, process,<br/>service & firewall APIs] -->|read-only| C[Collect-Windows.ps1<br/>PowerShell collector]
    C -->|token-authenticated<br/>loopback upload| S[Python server in Docker<br/>explainable review rules]
    S -->|polls every 5s| B[Browser dashboard<br/>HTML / CSS / JS]

title: Portlight: Local Network Security Dashboard
text:
Features

Review queue with High, Medium, Low, and Info priorities. Each finding shows the observed evidence, a confidence level, the reasoning, and suggested manual hardening steps.
Views for listening ports, live TCP connections, devices and services, and an evidence-and-limits page that separates what is observed, inferred, suspected, and unverified.
Search and filters by process, port, protocol, priority, and address scope, plus JSON export of snapshots.
Demo mode with a clear synthetic-data banner. Demo data is never silently substituted when collection fails.

title: Portlight: Local Network Security Dashboard
text:
Security and engineering choices

The container runs as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem, all Linux capabilities dropped, and no-new-privileges. It’s published on 127.0.0.1 only.
Uploads require a random 256-bit token, created at startup and passed through an environment variable, and they must include a valid, size-bounded JSON payload. The token never reaches browser JavaScript.
The front end has no CDNs, external fonts, or analytics, so nothing leaves the machine.
14 automated tests cover IPv4/IPv6 scope handling, listener matching, stale and partial data, firewall profiles, and authentication. They passed on Python 3.11 and inside a Python 3.13 container.

title: Predicting King County Home Prices
text:
Approach
1. Cleaning. I parsed the sale date into year and month, dropped ID columns, and removed implausible records: more than 15 bedrooms, bathroom counts outside 0.5–5.5, and extreme living and lot sizes.
2. Feature engineering. I used log transforms of square footage, living-to-lot and above-to-basement ratios, house age, years since renovation, and a renovation flag. K-means clusters on latitude and longitude capture neighborhood effects.
3. Model. I used an XGBoost regressor with an 80/20 train/test split, then ran the same cleaning function on the holdout set so the training and scoring data stay consistent.
def clean_housing(housing):
    housing['datetime'] = housing['date'].str.split('T').str[0]
    housing = housing.assign(
        year=housing['datetime'].str[0:4].astype(int),
        month=housing['datetime'].str[4:6].astype(int),
    ).drop(columns=['date', 'datetime', 'id'])

    clean = housing[housing['bedrooms'] <= 15]
    clean = clean[(clean['bathrooms'] <= 5.5) & (clean['bathrooms'] >= .5)]
    clean = clean[clean['sqft_living'] <= 8670]
    clean = clean[clean['sqft_lot'] <= 500000]
    return clean

model = XGBRegressor()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

title: Predicting King County Home Prices
text:
What I learned
Removing a small number of extreme listings improved the model more than adding extra engineered features did, cutting RMSE by about $23,000. Bundling the cleaning steps into a single function also made it simple to score new holdout files without mismatched columns.

This dataset comes from CMS and includes drug products that were newly reported during the week of October 20 through October 26, 2025. I downloaded the file straight from the Medicaid website so the report can be run again without having to manually download the data.

    `Drug Type`,
    `Unit Type`,

  mutate(drug_type_label = case_when(
      as.character(`Drug Type`) == "1" ~ "Prescription",
      as.character(`Drug Type`) == "2" ~ "Over-the-Counter",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"),
    unit_type_label = case_when(`Unit Type` == "AHF" ~ "Anti-Hemophilic Factor",

      `Unit Type` == "SUP" ~ "Suppository",
      `Unit Type` == "TAB" ~ "Tablet",

      TRUE ~ "Unknown"),
    `Drug Category` = as.factor(`Drug Category`),

    !is.na(match(split_result[,2], month.abb)) ~  match(split_result[,2], month.abb),

Show the code

  mutate(
    clean1 = as.numeric(clean1),
    clean2 = as.numeric(clean2),
    result = clean1 + clean2) %>%

Show the code
final <- math %>%
  mutate(final_sleep = ifelse(result > 11, result / 2, result)) %>% 
  select(-c(4,5,6,7,8))




Show the code

  mutate(caffine_status = ifelse(final$Beverage %in% c("Water","Milk","Juice","Sports drink","Soft drink (non-caffeinated)","Powdered drink", "other"), "Non-Caffine", "Caffine")) %>%

  H_0: \mu_\text{Non-Caffinated} = \mu_\text{Caffinated}
 
  H_a: \mu_\text{Non-Caffinated} \neq \mu_\text{Caffinated}


  \alpha = 0.05

title: Oreo Dissolving: Liquid × Temperature
text:
This experiment tested whether Oreo’s dissolve faster in different liquids and temperatures. More specifically, I wanted to see whether an Oreo would dissolve faster in water or Mountain Dew and whether the temperature of the liquid would have an effect on how much of the Oreo dissolved after one minute.
In order to test this, I designed an experiment using two factors: liquid type and temperature. The liquid type had two levels, water and Mountain Dew, while temperature had two levels, hot (100°F) and cold (50°F). This gave us four different treatment combinations. The response variable was the proportion of the Oreo remaining after one minute, represented by a decimal. A smaller decimal meant that more of the Oreo had dissolved. I wanted to determine whether either factor had an effect on dissolving and whether the two factors interacted with each other.

title: Oreo Dissolving: Liquid × Temperature
text:
Basic Statistics


Show the code
favstats(Degredation ~ Temp + Liquid, data = oreo)


        Temp.Liquid  min     Q1 median     Q3  max   mean        sd n missing
1 Cold.Mountain_Dew 0.05 0.0875  0.100 0.1625 0.35 0.1500 0.1354006 4       0
2  Hot.Mountain_Dew 0.50 0.5750  0.700 0.8500 1.00 0.7250 0.2217356 4       0
3        Cold.Water 0.05 0.0875  0.150 0.2375 0.35 0.1750 0.1322876 4       0
4         Hot.Water 0.60 0.7125  0.875 1.0000 1.00 0.8375 0.1973787 4       0


Show the code
boxplot(oreo$Degredation ~ Temp * Liquid, data = oreo, main = "Degredation amount of Oreos", xlab = "Degredation (%)", ylab = "Different Solutions", col = c("skyblue", "orange", "lightgreen", "red"))









Show the code
BF2oreo <- aov(Degredation ~ Temp * Liquid, data = oreo)


In order to describe the results, I compared the proportion of Oreo remaining after one minute for each of the four treatment combinations. There were 16 observations in total, with four observations for each combination of liquid and temperature. The overall average proportion of Oreo remaining was 0.47, with a standard deviation of 0.36. The smallest observed proportion remaining was 0.05 and the largest was 1.00.
The cold Mountain Dew had the lowest average proportion of Oreo remaining at 0.15, meaning that it dissolved the most Oreo during the one-minute period. The hot water had the highest average proportion remaining at 0.84 meaning that the Oreo dissolved the least in that solution.
Looking at the variation between observations, cold water had the smallest standard deviation, meaning that its results were the most consistent in this experiment. Meanwhile, hot mountain dew had the largest standard deviation, meaning that its observations varied the most between rounds.
The boxplot shows that the biggest difference in whether or not the Oreo dissolved wasn’t the type of solution but was the temperature of the solution. Although some treatments appeared to dissolve more Oreo than others, we will need to use an ANOVA to determine whether these differences provide statistically significant evidence of an effect.

title: Oreo Dissolving: Liquid × Temperature
text:
Interaction Plot


Show the code
interaction.plot(oreo$Temp, oreo$Liquid, oreo$Degredation, col = c("blue", "red"), xlab = "Temperature", ylab = "Mean Proportion of Oreo Remaining", trace.label = "Liquid", main = "Interaction Between Liquid and Temperature")









Before performing the ANOVA, I created an interaction plot to see whether the effect of temperature changed depending on the type of liquid being used. This is important because we want to determine not only whether temperature and liquid type have individual effects, but also whether they have an effect when combined.
The interaction plot shows that each has a positive slope from cold to hot and that they appear parallel. This suggests that there MAY NOT be an interaction between the two factors. However, we cannot determine whether this interaction is statistically significant from the plot alone, so we will use the ANOVA to test it.

title: Oreo Dissolving: Liquid × Temperature
text:
Checking the data


Show the code
par(mfrow = c(1,3))

plot(BF2oreo, which = 1)

plot(BF2oreo, which = 2)

qqPlot(BF2oreo$residuals)









[1] 14  9


Before interpreting the ANOVA, I checked the normality, variances, and residuals to determine whether the assumptions of the test were reasonable.
Looking at the residuals versus fitted values plot, our data looks to be valid because each residual is randomly placed and does not give a cone shape. The QQ plot shows that each data point follows the expected line for the residuals. I also compared the spread of the observations between the different treatment combinations and found that the data is normalize and therefor each point is valid.
Overall, the data appears to meet the assumptions of ANOVA. However, because there were only four observations per treatment combination and the remaining Oreo was measured using visual estimates, we should be cautious when interpreting the results.

title: Oreo Dissolving: Liquid × Temperature
text:
Anova


Show the code
summary(BF2oreo)


            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
Temp         1 1.5314  1.5314  49.417 1.38e-05 ***
Liquid       1 0.0189  0.0189   0.610    0.450    
Temp:Liquid  1 0.0077  0.0077   0.247    0.628    
Residuals   12 0.3719  0.0310                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


For the two-way ANOVA, I wanted to determine whether liquid type, temperature, or the interaction between the two factors had an effect on the average proportion of Oreo remaining after one minute. I used a significance level of 0.05.
The first null hypothesis was that there was no difference in the population mean proportion of Oreo remaining between water and Mountain Dew. The second null hypothesis was that there was no difference between hot and cold temperatures. The third null hypothesis was that there was no interaction between liquid type and temperature.
Interaction Effect
The ANOVA produced a p-value of 0.628 for the interaction between liquid type and temperature. Since this value is less than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis that there is no interaction between the two factors.
This suggests that we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude that the effect of temperature differs depending on the type of liquid being used. This also tells us that a pairwise comparison would not be helpful because their is no significant interaction between the two factors
Main Effect of Liquid Type
For the liquid type, the ANOVA produced a p-value of 0.45. Since this value is less than 0.05, we again fail to reject the null hypothesis that water and Mountain Dew have the same population mean proportion of Oreo remaining.
This means that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that water and Mountain Dew produce different average proportions of Oreo remaining.
Main Effect of Temperature
For temperature, the ANOVA produced a p-value of 0.0000138. Since this value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis that hot and cold liquids have the same population mean proportion of Oreo remaining.
This provides evidence that temperature has an effect on the proportion of Oreo remaining after one minute.

Background and Hypothesis
The following data was taken from individuals to understand attention span and how things like external stimuli and caffeine can affect attention. The data was collected as subjects participated in tests designed to show subjects reaction time. Each participant took the test with and without caffeine and with and without external stimuli. Caffeine content ranged from 0mg, 50mg, and 100mg, each taken 45 min prior to engaging with the test. External stimuli consisted of no stimuli, audio stimuli (in the form of random pop songs), visual stimuli (in which subjects watched a video of ping pong practice), and combined audio and visual stimuli (where both the video and the music were played).

Of the whole experiment, two factors can effect the reaction time of the participants which are caffeine intake and stimuli. An ANOVA test will be performed on the data using the following hypothesis

Conclusion
Each of these summaries come together to show us the understanding we need about our data and the relationship each factor has with the others. Our diagnostic plots show us the data we have collected from our participants is usable and consistent with general population data. This helps us to understand the validity of the further analysis we have done on the data. Our XYPlots help to show us the rough relationship that distractions and caffeine levels have with reaction times. Hypothesizing from the graphic plots we can go forward in our analysis. After concluding that we believe that their is a relationship between reaction time and caffeine intake levels and reaction time and outside distraction, we move onto our analysis. say that, using a two-way ANOVA, caffeine and different distraction inputs have a significant relationship on reaction time.
